content.text: The programme was implemented by a consortium of seven agencies of the Aga Khan Development Network, with funding provided by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade in Australia.

A leading agency in the implementation of the programme, IED's Professional Development Centre, North, worked with 59 schools, of which majority were public schools, using a cluster-based whole school improvement model.

The model was based on the features of the Whole School Improvement Programme, which is a signature school improvement programme of PDCN. The cluster-based model involved the transformation of one centrally based school into a Learning Resource School, with three others completing the cluster in the form of feeding units. This allowed the interaction of schools in a more cohesive way, making for more productive learning environments. "We saw the student enrolment levels rising by 40 per cent, from 7,524 in 2010 to 12,041 in 2014," says Dr Mola Dad Shafa, Head of PDCN. "Additionally, girls' enrolment in the target schools has gone up by 47 per cent as compared to the base year."

The primary aim of the programme was the provision of greater learning opportunities for  children living in the selected districts. For instance, the programme emphasized the enhancement of leadership and teaching skills of the faculty, as well as the effective engagement of the community and government education departments in school affairs.

Moreover, specific sessions were held with the families of students in order to foster greater familial involvement in the child's education. Despite the barrier of illiteracy, parents were invited to engage in discussions that aimed to help them understand how they could contribute to their children's education, inside and outside the classroom. For this purpose, parent-teacher meetings were introduced into the system, allowing parents to monitor and express interest in their child's progress. There were also special sessions held for grandparents, who were reminded that they were instrumental in the development of their grandchild's character, which in turn impacted their academic achievements. Another aim of the programme was to provide schools with basic resources such as stationery, text books, furniture and uniforms.

The programme also attempted to enrich  school curriculums through locally available resources so that students could comprehend topics more easily. For instance, while studying water pollution, students were taken outside and shown examples of water pollution in their own local environments, making the learning experience more effective and hands on.

The immediate outcomes of the programme indicate that the EDIP interventions have significantly improved the overall teaching and learning conditions. Schools once considered 'low quality', with teachers taking little interest in the service they were providing and the deteriorated conditions of the building, emerged as competitive players in the region's education sector. From broken floors and peeling plaster, and no interaction between parents and teachers, the implementation of EDIP allowed schools to claim awards and accolades for their performance. Three of the schools, including Government Boys High School Karimabad, Hunza, Government Girls Primary School Gitch, Punial, and Government Girls Primary School Jutial, Gilgit were even able to win the regional-level best school awards given by the government of Gilgit-Baltistan during 2014.

A major success for the programme was recorded in the Diamer district, which had the lowest levels of literacy with minimal female student enrolments. The inclusion of the Diamer district into EDIP helped Dr Shafa and his team to reverse the change-resistant attitudes and negative perceptions of the local community regarding education. The locals of the area had apprehensions about girls education and were distrustful and sensitive of NGO funding. However, they were gradually persuaded that the implementation of EDIP would have no negative implications whatsoever for the district and that the Project would help them progress like other areas in the region that had implemented the programme.

"The carefully-tailored implementation of EDIP in Diamer has not only helped AKDN make inroads in this resistant-to-change district, but has also helped the local communities broaden their worldview and become willing partners in their own socioeconomic development." Dr Shafa, spoke confidently about the ways in which the EDIP intervention in Diamer has brought about a change in attitudes and mind sets of the local people. He emphasized how the initial resistance was replaced by a growing, enthusiastic support for change, and apprehensions about donor involvement turning into trusting partnerships working for educational development. Locals in the area were able to look past their hostility towards outsiders and accepted them as friends and well-wishers, working with them in their best interests.

content.title: Marked improvement
content.author: Iqra Paintern
content.description: The five-year Educational Development and Improvement Programme in the Gilgit-Baltistan region was successfully completed today. The programme complemented the efforts of the provincial government to enhance access, equity, improve the quality of education and augment its relevance in the region.
